# Version control with `git`

This section will be on the homework but I won't put it on the exams.

## Introduction

The setup guide explains the `git add` - `git commit` - `git push` idiom to hand in your labs. In this unit we look at what those commands actually do, and at the handful of other commands that you will likely use if you pursue data science / engineering.

`git` keeps a complete history of a folder of files (hence why it's great for teams working on text files housing code, i.e., for "version control"). Every saved snapshot is called a **commit**; it has an author, a date, a message, and a short identifying alphanumeric code e.g., `a1b2c3d`. Nothing in a commit is ever silently overwritten, which is why `git` is such a good safety net.

`git` is not the only version control system, but it is the dominant one by far. Nobody counts "worldwide users" of a free tool exactly, so the best we have is the share of developers who say they use each one in surveys (people can name several, so shares can add to more than 100%).

+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
| System           | Born | Model       | Share of developers     | Where you meet it         |
|                  |      |             | (approx.)               |                           |
+:=================+=====:+:============+========================:+:==========================+
| `git`            | 2005 | distributed | ~94%                    | Almost everything,        |
|                  |      |             |                         | including `git` itself    |
+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
| Subversion (SVN) | 2000 | centralized | ~5%                     | Older companies and some  |
|                  |      |             |                         | academic groups           |
+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
| Perforce         | 1995 | centralized | a few % (no clean data) | Game studios, huge binary |
|                  |      |             |                         | assets                    |
+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
| Mercurial (`hg`) | 2005 | distributed | ~1%                     | Legacy projects (Mozilla  |
|                  |      |             |                         | moved to git)             |
+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
| CVS              | 1990 | centralized | ~0% (legacy projects    | Museum piece; SVN was     |
|                  |      |             | only)                   | built to replace it       |
+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+

: Version control systems, ordered by share of developers. Survey figures are approximate and the 2025 numbers are secondhand (via [RhodeCode's summary](https://rhodecode.com/insights) of the Stack Overflow survey); Perforce and CVS have no reliable current figure, so their order is a rough judgement from [a Gartner legacy-project poll](https://www.gartner.com/peer-community/poll/what-version-control-system-vcs-are-you-using-for-legacy-projects).


# GitHub

`git` is the tool; GitHub is a website/company (owned by Microsoft) that hosts `git` repositories (which are called the "remotes" and are usually named `origin`, `master`, `main`). GitHub also manages "pull requests" (PRs), issue tracking and so on. Here is a list of places where `git` is served:

+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+
| Host                 | Owner     | Accounts (approx.) | Notes                                |
+:=====================+:==========+===================:+:=====================================+
| GitHub               | Microsoft | ~180M              | Largest by far; where our course     |
|                      |           |                    | repo lives                           |
+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+
| Self-hosted servers  | companies | ~20-40M (guess)    | Private servers; overlaps other rows |
+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+
| GitLab               | GitLab    | ~30M (unreliable)  | Popular to self-host inside          |
|                      |           |                    | companies                            |
+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+
| Bitbucket            | Atlassian | ~15M               | Integrates with Jira; dropped        |
|                      |           |                    | Mercurial support                    |
+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+
| Azure DevOps, others | various   | no public figure   | Common in Microsoft shops,           |
|                      |           |                    | SourceForge is the old-timer         |
+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+

: Git hosting services, ordered by accounts. GitHub's figure is from its 2025 Octoverse report (via [secondary coverage](https://www.getpanto.ai/blog/github-statistics)); Bitbucket's is Atlassian's 2025 "developers" count; GitLab's is an undated third-party estimate. Accounts are not active users, and one person may hold several. The self-hosted row is my own order-of-magnitude guess, not a measurement: no one publishes a total, so it assumes a large share of GitLab's accounts and most of Bitbucket's enterprise users sit on company-run servers. Private repos kept on GitHub itself are not counted. 

GitHub is the biggest venue for open source software in the world. Most of the projects we met in the previous section keep their code there: [Python](https://github.com/python/cpython), [R](https://github.com/wch/r-source) (a mirror, see below), [Linux](https://github.com/torvalds/linux) (also a mirror), [`pandas`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas), [`NumPy`](https://github.com/numpy/numpy), [`TensorFlow`](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow), [`PyTorch`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch), [`Kubernetes`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes), [`VS Code`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode) and [Quarto](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli), [`git`](https://github.com/git/git) itself, along with millions of smaller libraries. Even projects that develop elsewhere keep a mirror on GitHub, such as the Linux kernel (developed through mailing lists), R (developed in Subversion) and [PostgreSQL](https://github.com/postgres/postgres) (which runs its own git server), because that is where people look for code. It became the default for three reasons:

* **Network effect:** with about 180 million developers, a project on GitHub is where its potential users and contributors already are.
* **Low friction:** anyone can **fork** (copy) a public project (i.e. in a repo), change it and propose the change back with a **pull request**, with no permission needed. Issues, discussion and automated testing live on the same page.
* **Visibility:** search, **stars** and your commit history on your profile make GitHub a public CV, and employers often look at it. In a 2017 [HackerRank survey](https://www.hackerrank.com/research/developer-skills/2018), most hiring managers said they look for proven skill such as previous work and projects/GitHub, and in interviews with employers ([Marlow and Dabbish, 2013](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262248832_Activity_traces_and_signals_in_software_developer_recruitment_and_hiring)) they said they trust visible activity more than résumé claims. Microsoft bought GitHub in 2018 for about $7.5B likely because they wanted to buy the network of all the developers.

That is also why you hand in your labs by using `git` on GitHub it: the habits you build in this course are the ones used by open source projects everywhere and companies everywhere. You are learning the standard for any sort of software engineering and data science. And this is why I'm using class time to teach it. I wish someone taught it to me rather than having to learn it by trial and error and many lost hours.
