## Demo rules
I'll run every command below in the actual 52002 course repository. The first demo, a live commit and push of this very lecture file, is real. Everything after it happens only on **throw-away "branches"** that we delete at the end, so `main` is never touched by it (`main` is the production code for that runs this course) Two rules for the throw-away part that I'll stick to: never `git push` those branches, and use explicit file names with `git add` (not `git commit -a`), because our working folder may hold other unfinished changes.
:::

## The places a change travels through

A change to a file passes through several places on its way to GitHub:

```
 working folder     staging area      local repository   GitHub (the mothership - for sharing with others)
  (your files)      (next commit)      (your history)     (remote: origin)
        |                 |                   |                   |
        |---- git add ---->                   |                   |
        |                 |--- git commit ---->                   |
        |                 |                   |---- git push ----->
        |                 |                   |                   |
        <----------------------- git pull ------------------------|
```

Each level is confusing. The *staging area* lets you choose exactly which changes go into the next commit: `add` puts changes into the staging area, `commit` saves what is staged as one snapshot. And `git status` tells you what is where. Finally, `push` sends it to the mothership.

## The everyday loop

**Live demo: commit and push this lecture.** Let's save the file you are reading to GitHub. Add a blank line at the end of the lecture file (any whitespace will do). First we take a look at what is gitignored.

```bash
#do not run the commands in this chunk on your machine --- this is for me, the owner of the course repo only
cd ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026
```

Now we walk through the add-commit-push path. 

```bash
git status                          # which branch am I on (we'll discuss this soon)? what has changed in this branch?
#I'm going to make an edit in this file (delete a word, add a word, add a blank line)
git status
git diff --stat                        # which files changed, how, and by how many lines
git diff --ignore-blank-lines --stat   # git can also ignore blank lines: our line no longer counts
git diff                               #see the diff itself (additions are colored green and subtractions are colored red)
git add lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd   # stage just that file ("git add ."" means stage all files that were edited)
git diff                               #clean as diff measures difference between
git diff --staged                      # but the change is in the staging area: this is what the next commit would contain
git restore --staged lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd   # undo the staging (old spelling: git reset lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd); our edit stays in the file
git status                             # "Changes not staged for commit" again
git diff                               # and the change is back in the diff
git add lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd   # stage it again, to go on

git commit -m "lec03: small changes and whitespace, live git demo"
git push                            # upload; now refresh the file's page on GitHub
git log --oneline -n 3              # our commit is on top
#the top line should be
#<commit code> (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) lec03: whitespace, live git demo 
#now I'll open https://github.com/kapelner/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026 and click on "commits" and look at the diff
```

What do these things mean?

HEAD: the current branch, and through it the current commit
main            your local branch (moves when you commit)
origin/main and origin/HEAD we'll discuss later if we have time

Each commit contains all files compressed at that specific point in history (if the file doesn't change between commits, it just points to a previous commit so it's not actually wasteful). This makes it very fast to "checkout" code at any point. But this is the reason saving large files that constantly change is NOT a good idea. This is why large files should be gitignored!

You can design the system to just save the diffs each time and then replay the diffs at every point in history (CVS, SVN) but git chooses to be faster for checkout.


A couple conveniences I use constantly:

* `git add .` stages *everything* in the folder that is not ignored. Run `git status` first. If you don't check the status, then you make mistakes e.g. a 35 MB `covid.csv` ends up in a repository by accident.
* `git commit -am "msg"` does `git add <all staged>` then commits with a message stages every change to files git **already tracks**, but it skips **new** files. That is why the setup guide runs `git add .` first: it stages new files too.
* Write commit messages that say *what and why* ("fix off-by-one in header skip"), not "stuff" or "asdf". You will need to read them in six months from now and you won't remember what you did. Also, if you work with other people, they will need to read them immediately.

Remember: once you hit `git push`, it sends your new commits to GitHub, the mothership for your code that is indelibly recorded forever (see [my github page](https://github.com/kapelner) and click "arctic") that your teammates can access.

What will likely not be useful `git` commands for you in this class:

* `git pull` brings other people's (or your other computer's) commits down. Pull before you start working, and push when you are done. Since nobody else is pushing to your repo, there is nothing ever to pull!
* Set your working directory to your main worksapce folder then `git init <new repo_name>` creates a new repo on your local machine. Useful for you own tracking. There's no mothership unless you connect it to one. `git` can work without a mothership. But if Zohar's cat eats your computer... Also, don't run `git init` inside a folder that is already inside another repo, because that creates a repo within a repo. That's a huge mess... To connect your local repo to the mothership, make a new repo on the mothership then use `git remote add origin <url>`.


## What is a branch?

A **branch** is a separate line of development. You can think of it as a parallel copy of the project in which you can edit, commit and break things without affecting anyone else's copy. If the experiment works, you **merge** it back; if it doesn't, you delete the branch and nothing is lost.

Under the hood a branch is not a copy at all. It is just a **movable label that points to one commit** (a tiny file with a commit code in it), so creating a branch is instant and costs nothing, even for a huge project. When you commit, the label of the branch you are on moves forward to the new commit. `HEAD` (the "where am I?" pointer from before) says which branch is the current one:

```
                 C---D         <- lec03-demo   (a branch we are experimenting on)
                /
        A---B---E---F          <- main         (the production code, untouched)
                    ^
                   HEAD  (if we are standing on main)
```

Here the two lines share the history A--B and then go their own ways: `main` kept going with E and F, and `lec03-demo` has its own commits C and D. Nothing that happens on one line shows up on the other until we merge.

Why use them?

* **Safety:** `main` always holds working code (in this course, the code that builds the website and the labs). Experiments happen elsewhere.
* **Parallel work:** several people (or you, on two ideas) work at the same time without stepping on each other. This is how teams of thousands of developers share one repository.
* **Review:** a branch is what you hand to a colleague in a pull request for review before it is merged into `main`.

The few commands we need:

```bash
git branch                    # list the branches; * marks the current one
git switch -c new-name        # create a branch and move onto it (-c = create)
git switch main               # move back to an existing branch (your files change to match it!)
git branch -d new-name        # delete a merged branch (-D forces it if it still has unmerged commits)
```

Now we can play with the undo commands safely.

**Live demo: three ways to undo.** We play on a throw-away branch so `main` is never touched. First, make a good commit and then a bad one:

```bash
git switch -c undo-demo                    # throw-away branch to play on
echo "good line" > notes.txt
git status
git add notes.txt
git status
git commit -m "add notes"
git status
echo "BAD line" >> notes.txt
git status
git commit -am "oops: a bad line"
cat notes.txt
git status
git log --oneline -n 3                     # the bad commit is on top
```

**Going back in time.** Because every commit is a complete snapshot, it's easy to "go back in time" if you feel like you messed something up. Going back one step just means pointing git at the commit below ours in `git log`. We first check to ensure this is where we want to rewind to:

```bash
git log --oneline -n 3
git show --stat HEAD~1          # "one commit before HEAD" (HEAD~2 is two before, and so on) which is equivalent to using the commit code
```

`git show` only *looks*. To put the whole working folder back to that point, we need to undo. There are a few types based on what you specifically want to do:

* To undo a commit by adding a *new* commit that undoes the previous commit, use `git revert`. History is only added to, so this is the safe choice for pushed commits. Reverting D gives a new commit D' where D' undoes D to get back to C (to get back to B, revert twice, etc):

  ```
  A->B->C->D   --git revert D-->   A->B->C->D->D' (where D' is the anti-D, reversing it so we arrive at state-of-affairs C)
  ```

* To rewrite history and get the branch's old state back, use `git reset --mixed` or `git reset --hard`. C and D will no longer be on the branch so you are destroying the work in C and D

  ```
  A->B->C->D   --git reset --mixed B-->   A->B   (files still contain C's and D's changes, un-staged)
  A->B->C->D   --git reset --hard B-->    A->B   (any work in C and D is destroyed permanently)
  ```

* To bring back just one file, use `git restore`. It changes your working folder, not the commit history:

  ```
  A->B->C->D   --git restore file-->   A->B->C->D   (only the file in the working folder changes)
  ```

I can demo these different types of "undo" but I don't want to mess up the course repo! So we take a slight detour now to talk about branches first.


`git revert` undoes a commit by making a **new** commit that does the opposite. History is only added to, never rewritten, so it is the safe choice for anything you have already pushed:

```bash
git revert HEAD                            # new commit "Revert 'oops: a bad line'"
git log --oneline -n 4                     # the bad commit is still there, followed by its undo
cat notes.txt                              # the BAD line is gone
```

`git restore` fixes **files**, not history. It never moves the branch:

```bash
echo "scribble" >> notes.txt
cat notes.txt
git status
git restore notes.txt                      # throw away uncommitted edits: the file is back to the last commit (cannot be undone!)
cat notes.txt
echo "scribble" >> notes.txt
cat notes.txt
git add -a notes.txt
git status

git restore -staged notes.txt              # copy the file as it was one commit ago (the BAD version) into the working folder
git restore notes.txt                      # throw away uncommitted edits
git status                                 # should be clean
```

`git reset` **moves the branch** back to an earlier commit and, depending on the option, what happens to your edits. Let's drop the revert commit and then the bad commit:

```bash
echo "scribble" >> notes.txt
git commit -am "made a bad scribble"
git log --oneline -n 3                     # bad commit atop
git reset --hard HEAD~1                    # branch moves back, scribble is gone but everything else you were working on as well
cat notes.txt
git log --oneline -n 3                     # no more bad commit - it's struck from history
```

Now let's show the preferred route:

```bash
echo "scribble" >> notes.txt
git commit -am "made a bad scribble"
git reset --soft HEAD~1                    # branch moves back, but the change stays STAGED
cat notes.txt                              # but the scribble is still there - what happened? We move back but previous commit is in staging area
git status                                 # "Changes to be committed": notes.txt still has the BAD line
git reset notes.txt                        # un-stage it (--mixed is the default): the change stays in the file, but not staged
git status                                 # "Changes not staged for commit"
cat notes.txt                              # just the good line
```

Because `reset` rewrites history, don't use it on commits you have already pushed (use `revert` for those). There is also a temporary "visit a previous commit" which can be done with `git switch --detach <commit>`, `HEAD` points straight at a commit instead of at a branch (a **detached HEAD**), as if you were visiting the old snapshot. It is safe for looking around, since `main` has not moved. Don't commit while detached: a commit made there belongs to no branch and will be lost when switching back to another branch. If you want to start work from the old snapshot, you can start a branch in the detached mode.

Clean up the playground:

```bash
git switch main
git branch -D undo-demo                    # delete the throw-away branch (-D because it was never merged)
```

## What git should not hold: `.gitignore`

Git is made for code and small text files. It is **not** made for big data: every version of a file is stored forever, and GitHub rejects any single file over 100 MB. Data, results and scratch files are kept out of the repository with a plain-text file called `.gitignore`, which lives in the repository (so it is versioned and shared like any other file). Each line is a pattern for files git should pretend not to see. Our own repo already has one:

```bash
vi .gitignore                  # includes the scratch/ line you added in Lab 1
git status --ignored            # also list what is being ignored
git check-ignore -v scratch/lec03/covid.csv   # WHICH rule ignores this file? (prints the file and line)
```

The pattern rules are short:

+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| Line in `.gitignore` | Meaning                                       |
+:=====================+:==============================================+
| `# comment`          | a comment; blank lines are skipped            |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `*.csv`              | any file ending in `.csv`, in any folder      |
|                      | (`*` matches any characters, but not `/`)     |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `scratch/`           | a folder (the trailing `/`) and everything    |
|                      | inside it, wherever it is                     |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `/data.csv`          | only `data.csv` in the top folder of the repo |
|                      | (a leading `/` anchors the pattern)           |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `**/old/`            | a folder called `old` at any depth            |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `!keep.csv`          | an **exception**: do not ignore `keep.csv`,   |
|                      | even if an earlier line ignored it            |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+

The last rule is read top to bottom and the last matching line wins, so put exceptions after the pattern they relax:


```bash
git status --ignored                          # also list what is being ignored
git check-ignore -v scratch/lec03/covid.csv   # audit: which rule ignores this file? (prints the file and line)
```

Three things trip people up:

* **Ignoring does not untrack.** `.gitignore` only affects files git is *not yet* tracking. If you already committed `covid.csv`, adding it to `.gitignore` changes nothing. Tell git to stop tracking it, and leave the file on disk:

```bash
echo "bigggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggggg" > big.csv
git status
git add big.csv                 # oops: a data file gets added...
git commit -m "oops, committed data"
echo "big.csv" >> .gitignore    # ...adding it to .gitignore now does nothing: git already tracks it
git status --ignored            # it's not being ignored! 
git rm --cached big.csv         # stop tracking; the file stays in the folder
git status --ignored            # now it's ignored
git add .gitignore && git commit -m "stop tracking big.csv"
rm big.csv                      # (demo only) delete the leftover file
git status
 ```

The file is still in the *old* commits. Removing a big file from the history is a harder job (a tool such as `git filter-repo`), so it is much better to check `git status` before every commit.
* **Ignore rules are per repository.** Junk that belongs to *your* machine and editor (`.DS_Store`, `*.swp`, `.vscode/`) can go in a personal global file instead of every project's `.gitignore`: `git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global`.
* **Empty folders are not tracked.** Git tracks files, not folders. The usual trick to keep an empty folder is a placeholder file inside it, e.g. `data/.gitkeep`, plus the lines `data/*` and `!data/.gitkeep` in `.gitignore`.

## Merging branches

We went over that a **branch** is a separate line of commits. It lets you try something (a new analysis, a risky rewrite) without touching the main line. When you are sure this work is correct, you can join it back to main; this is called a "merge".

```bash
git branch                          # list branches (the current one has a *)
git switch -c lec03-development     # new branch, and move onto it
                                    # (= `git branch lec03-exp` to create it, then `git switch lec03-exp`)
echo "an idea" >> demo_notes.txt
git commit -m "try an idea" demo_notes.txt
git switch main                     # back: demo_notes.txt no longer has the idea!
git branch 
git merge lec03-development         # bring the experiment's commits in
ls
rm demo_notes.txt                   # cleanup so we don't pollute production branch
git branch -d lec03-development     # delete a branch you are done with
git status
```

## Resolving conflicts

Git can combine two sets of changes automatically as long as they touch *different* parts of a file. This happens when you merge a branch into `main`, and also when you `git pull` (a pull is just a `git fetch` from remote followed by a `git merge`). A **conflict** happens when both sides changed the *same lines* in different ways. `git` cannot guess which version you want, so it stops, marks the problem lines in the file, and leaves you to decide. For example:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
from demo
=======
from fix
>>>>>>> lec03-fix
```

Everything between `<<<<<<<` and `=======` is your side, and the rest up to `>>>>>>>` is the other branch's side. To resolve it, edit the file into what you want (and delete the three marker lines), then finish the merge:

```bash
#edit the conflict.txt file by hand using your IDE or text editor like vi
git add conflict.txt
git commit                          # git suggests a merge message; save and close the editor
```

If you panic in the middle of a merge, `git merge --abort` puts everything back as it was before.

## `stash`: put your work aside

You are in the middle of an edit, and you need to switch branches or pull, but git refuses because of your uncommitted changes. You do not want to commit half-finished work. `git stash` puts **all** your uncommitted changes (in our repo that includes the lecture file we are editing!) in a drawer and gives you back a clean folder:

```bash
echo "half-finished thought" >> demo_notes.txt
git stash                           # shelve the changes; the folder is clean again
git status                          # nothing to commit
git switch lec03-fix                # switching is easy now
git switch lec03-demo
git stash list                      # what is in the drawer
git stash pop                       # take the newest stash out and re-apply it
git restore demo_notes.txt          # drop the half-finished thought; we only needed it for the demo
```

Useful variants: `git stash -u` also shelves *new* (untracked) files, which a plain `stash` leaves behind; `git stash push -m "wip: header fix" file1` shelves only `file1` and labels the stash; `git stash apply` re-applies but keeps the stash in the drawer; `git stash drop` throws a stash away.

## `worktree`: a second folder, same repository

`stash` is for a quick interruption. For a longer one (a hotfix while your analysis is half-done, or comparing two versions of a script side by side) a **worktree** is cleaner: a second folder, with its own branch checked out, that shares the same history as your main folder. Nothing in your main folder is disturbed.

+------------+------------------------+----------------------------+------------------+
| Tool       | What it holds          | Lifetime                   | Shared with      |
|            |                        |                            | GitHub?          |
+:===========+:=======================+:===========================+:=================+
| `stash`    | Uncommitted edits, put | Temporary: meant to be     | Never            |
|            | in a drawer            | popped within minutes or   |                  |
|            |                        | hours                      |                  |
+------------+------------------------+----------------------------+------------------+
| `worktree` | A second folder with a | As long as the folder      | Only through its |
|            | branch checked out     | exists; remove it when     | branch           |
|            |                        | done                       |                  |
+------------+------------------------+----------------------------+------------------+
| `branch`   | A line of commits      | Permanent until you delete | Yes, if you push |
|            |                        | it                         | it               |
+------------+------------------------+----------------------------+------------------+

: Three ways to set work aside. A worktree is a place to work and needs a branch; a stash is not a commit on any branch.

A rule of thumb:

- **Stash:** "I'll be back in five minutes."
- **Worktree:** "I need a second workspace while this one stays as it is."
- **Branch:** "This is a real line of work I'll keep and merge."

```bash
git worktree add ../lec03-wt -b lec03-wt    # new folder next to the repo, on a new branch
git worktree list                           # every folder attached to this repo
cd ../lec03-wt                              # work, commit and run things here as usual
cd -                                        # back to the main folder: its files never changed
git worktree remove ../lec03-wt             # done: delete the folder (--force if it has changes)
git branch -D lec03-wt                      # the branch is separate; delete it too
```

It is far cheaper than a second `git clone`, since the history is stored only once. Two rules: a branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time, and always remove a worktree with `git worktree remove` (if you just delete the folder, `git worktree prune` clears the leftover record). Tools like Claude Code use throw-away worktrees to try changes without touching your files.

Ensure we're clean

```bash
git stash list                      # should be empty (or only stashes that are really yours)
git switch main                     # back to the real branch
git worktree list                   # should show only the main folder
git status                          # back to exactly where we started
```


# Tabular data and its types

Everything so far in this course focused on the CSV: plain text, one row per line. Before we look for a better file format, we should say precisely what kind of data a CSV holds, because the kind of data decides what a good format for it looks like. This unit defines **tabular data** (rows and columns) and the **types** of the values in a column. The next unit uses both words to motivate a new file format.

Make a scratch folder for this lecture and bring the data along (we use it again in the database unit):

```bash
mkdir -p ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03
cd ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03
cp ../lec01/covid.csv .
ls -alh
```

## What is "tabular data" or a "data table" or a "table"?

A CSV holds **tabular data**, so let us define it. A table is a rectangle with two directions. Because everyone uses data, there are many equivalent English vocabulary terms:

* Each **row** is one **object** (AKA a subject, an observation, a case, a record, a unit, an example, an instance and others): one thing that we measured.
* Each **column** is one **attribute** (AKA a feature, a characteristic, a variable, a field, a predictor and others): one property that we measured, for every object. 

Usually the # of rows is denoted $n$ and the number of columns denoted $p$.

Every row has the same columns, and every column holds one kind of value (all dates, or all integers, or all text). Here are the first rows of `covid.csv`:

```bash
head -n 4 covid.csv | column -s, -t
```

The six columns are the attributes. Each row is one object. What is the definition of object in this table data set?









Here the *object* is the **report for one county on one day**: "Snohomish County on 2020-01-21". The object is *not* a county, since Snohomish appears in many rows (`date`, `county` and `state` together identify a row, because many states have a Washington County), and deciding what one row stands for is the first question to ask of any dataset. In this context, the vocabulary I would use is "this file has 884,737 records and 6 fields per record".

In science, there are generally two goals when using data: prediction or inference (we will see these topics later). If you are operating under one of these goals, there is one (sometimes more than one) column that is special. Because there are many fields of science that operate under these two goals and they emerged independently, there are once again many equivalent English vocabulary terms. This special column is called the **output** (AKA endpoint, outcome, response, label and others) of interest. And the other columns then are called **inputs** (AKA covariates, regressors, predictors and others)

Is our goal to predict anything? Are we explaining anything? Is there an output of interest?









We were given no prediction or inference frame. Hence there is no special column that is distinguished as the response.

Here is a table that summarizes the vocabulary terms across fields. There's a lot of words!!

+------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
|                  | Rows                         | Columns                                                               |
|                  |                              +--------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
|                  |                              | inputs (the $X$s)                    | output (the $y$)               |
+:=================+:=============================+:=====================================+:===============================+
| Statistics       | subjects, observations,      | independent variables, predictors,   | dependent variable, response,  |
|                  | units, cases                 | covariates, explanatory variables    | outcome                        |
+------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Machine learning | examples, instances,         | features, attributes, inputs (the    | label, target, output (the     |
|                  | samples, data points         | $X$s)                                | $y$)                           |
+------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Econometrics     | observations, units          | regressors, explanatory variables,   | regressand, dependent          |
|                  | (individuals, firms,         | independent variables, covariates,   | variable, outcome              |
|                  | countries)                   | controls                             |                                |
+------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Psychology       | participants, subjects,      | independent variables (what the      | dependent variable (the        |
|                  | cases                        | experimenter manipulates),           | measured outcome), scale score |
|                  |                              | predictors, items (one per survey    |                                |
|                  |                              | question)                            |                                |
+------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Sociology        | respondents, cases, units of | independent variables, covariates,   | dependent variable, outcome    |
|                  | analysis                     | indicators                           |                                |
+------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Physics          | events, measurements, runs,  | independent variables (what is set   | dependent variables,           |
|                  | data points                  | or varied), controlled quantities    | observables (what is           |
|                  |                              |                                      | measured), channels            |
+------------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Databases        | records, tuples              | fields, attributes (no special output column)                         |
+------------------+------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| R / Python       | rows of a data frame         | columns of a data frame (no special output column)                    |
+------------------+------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+

: The same rectangle, in several vocabularies. You will see all of them in this course.

Not all data is tabular. E.g.

* A nested JSON record (e.g., `{"name": "Kapelner", "address": {"city": "London"}, "langs": ["R", "Python"]}`, which has a record inside a record and a list inside a record), 
* an image, 
* a sound clip,
* a video,
* a paragraph of text is not a rectangle of objects by attributes. 

For now, we will be focusing on tables. We will see how far we get. I would love to cover handling big data for non-tabular datasets. As for the nested JSON record, we will be kind of covering nested tables / joins when we get to multi-table datasets.

## Data types (= column types)

Every column has a **type**: the kind of thing its values are, which decides what you are allowed to do with them. There are two layers to keep apart. The first is what the values *mean* (the statistical type), and the second is how the computer *stores* them (the storage type).

**What the values mean.** The classical scheme sorts a column by the operations that make sense on it:

+------------------+------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
| Type             | Subtype                | Example                | What makes sense           | In `covid.csv` |
+:=================+:=======================+:=======================+:===========================+:===============+
| **Categorical**  | **nominal**: which     | state, blood type,     | equal or not equal;        | `state`,       |
| (a fixed set of  | group?                 | country                | counting; no order         | `county`       |
| levels)          +------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
|                  | **ordinal**: which     | grade (A, B, C), shirt | order (<, >), but the gaps | none           |
|                  | group, in a *ranked*   | size (S, M, L),        | between levels are not     |                |
|                  | order?                 | "disagree / neutral /  | meaningful                 |                |
|                  |                        | agree"                 |                            |                |
+------------------+------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
| **Numeric**      | **ratio, continuous**: | height, weight,        | everything: differences    | none           |
| (arithmetic      | how much?              | income, time spent,    | *and* ratios, because zero |                |
| makes sense, at  |                        | temperature in Kelvin  | means "none" (20 kg is     |                |
| least in part)   |                        |                        | twice 10 kg)               |                |
|                  +------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
|                  | **ratio, discrete**:   | number of cases,       | everything a ratio allows, | `cases`,       |
|                  | how many whole things? | children in a family,  | but the values are only    | `deaths`       |
|                  | (a **count**)          | clicks on a page       | the whole numbers 0, 1, 2, |                |
|                  |                        |                        | ... (never 1.5)            |                |
|                  +------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
|                  | **interval**: how far  | temperature in         | differences (30°C is 10°   | `date`         |
|                  | apart?                 | Celsius, a calendar    | warmer than 20°C), but no  |                |
|                  |                        | date                   | ratios: the zero is        |                |
|                  |                        |                        | arbitrary, so 30°C is not  |                |
|                  |                        |                        | "1.5 times as hot" as 20°C |                |
+------------------+------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
| **Text /**       |                        | a tweet, an address, a | search and parse it; not a | none           |
| **character**    |                        | comment                | categorical until you      |                |
| (free text):     |                        |                        | extract the L categories   |                |
| what was         |                        |                        |                            |                |
| written?         |                        |                        |                            |                |
+------------------+------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+

: The statistical types. A **categorical** column has a fixed set of levels (nominal or ordinal), and a **numeric** column holds numbers (interval or ratio). A count is a ratio that is **discrete** (only whole numbers); the other numeric subtypes are **continuous**.

A few places where this is not obvious:

```bash
head -n 4 covid.csv | column -s, -t
```

* **A code that looks like a number is nominal.** `fips` is made of digits, but adding two FIPS codes or taking their mean is meaningless. It is a label for a county, so it should be stored as text. (In the next unit we will watch a program silently turn the code `06059` into `6059`.)
* **Discrete and continuous are both numeric, but they behave differently.** `cases` can be 0, 1, 2, but never 1.5, so it is a discrete count. A measured quantity such as height is continuous. Both have a true zero, but you use different models for them, and they are stored differently (integer versus decimal, see "Parquet's data types" below).
* **A yes/no column is a special case**, called binary. It is nominal or ordinal with exactly two levels (stored as `true` / `false`). It is also a count with 0 or 1.
* **Ordinal data is the one most often mishandled.** If you store grades A, B, C as 1, 2, 3, a program will happily average them, and it will treat the step from A to B as the same size as the step from B to C. Keep the order, but do not do arithmetic on them.
* **Missing values are part of the type.** In `covid.csv`, 8,266 rows have no `fips` (mostly the county `Unknown`, plus a few cities) and 18,761 rows have no `deaths`. A column of integers cannot hold "missing" in many programs.

```bash
#date,county,state,fips,cases,deaths
awk -F, 'NR>1 && $4=="" && $2=="Unknown"' covid.csv | head -n 10
awk -F, 'NR>1 && $4=="" && $2=="Unknown" {u++} END {print u}' covid.csv
```

A CSV stores all of these types (and subtypes) as text and leaves every program to guess the storage type, which is what goes wrong with `fips`. A better file format would store the type with the data, so that a `date` stays a date, `cases` stays an integer and `fips` stays text (so you can't take accidentally compute the nonsensical average of a bunch of `fips` values). For a nominal column such as `state`, with 55 distinct values repeated on 885,000 rows, it could store the small list of levels once and then a short code per row (**dictionary encoding**), which also makes the column small in contribution to file size. The same idea in R is a `factor` and in `pandas` is a `category`.

+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| Statistical type     | Typical storage type | R                    | `pandas`             |
+:=====================+:=====================+:=====================+:=====================+
| nominal              | text, or a           | `character`,         | `object` / `string`, |
|                      | dictionary of levels | `factor`             | `category`           |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| ordinal              | the same, with the   | `ordered` factor     | ordered `category`   |
|                      | level order recorded |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| interval or ratio, a | decimal ("floating   | `numeric`            | `float64`            |
| measurement          | point")              |                      |                      |
| (Celsius, height,    |                      |                      |                      |
| income)              |                      |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| count                | integer              | `integer`            | `int64`              |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| date or time         | a date or a          | `Date`, `POSIXct`    | `datetime64`         |
|                      | timestamp            |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| binary               | boolean              | `logical`            | `bool`               |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| character (free      | text                 | `character`          | `object` / `string`  |
| text)                |                      |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+

: Storage types of the data types in R and Python

Notice that programs do not distinguish interval from ratio: both are stored as decimals, and the difference exists only in what you may sensibly compute with them (a ratio of two Celsius temperatures is a number, but a meaningless one). What programs *do* distinguish is integer from decimal (`integer` versus `numeric` in R, `int64` versus `float64` in `pandas`), which is why counts get their own row. A date is stored as a number of days since a fixed starting day, with a label that says to show it as a date.

# A better data format than CSV?

The CSV is the universal format for tabular data, and you will receive data in it for the rest of your career. But a CSV is just the bare table: no column types, nothing about what is inside, and no way to read part of it without reading all of it. Before we go all the way to a database, there is a middle step that is still just a file you can copy, send to others and commit in your repo if it's small enough: **Parquet**. Parquet in French means "small space / room / compartment" because it's compressed down and tidied.

Think of Parquet as **annotated tabular data**. It stores the same table as the CSV, plus notes about the table, written into the file itself: the name and type of every column, how each column was compressed, and a summary (the smallest and largest value) of every block of rows. Those annotations are what make it

* **fast to read**: a program knows the types in advance, so it does not parse and guess, and it can read just the columns it needs, and
* **fast to query**: the summaries let a program skip the blocks that cannot contain the answer without even reading them.

This unit motivates the annotated format, converts `covid.csv`, and then shows what happens when the data is really large: it keeps working, in R and in Python, when the CSV would not even fit in memory.

## What is wrong with a CSV?

Three complaints that need no database at all:

1. **It is big.** Text spends one byte per digit and writes `Texas` out again on 67,002 rows. Our `covid.csv` is 35 MB, and `gzip` can squeeze it to 9 MB, but then every tool must unpack it first.
2. **It has no types.** A CSV does not know that `date` is a date, that `cases` is an integer, or that `fips` is a numeric *code* but not actually a number. Every program guesses on every read. Guess `fips` is an integer and the code `06059` (Orange County, California) silently becomes `6059`. Compare what the two languages guess on the same file:

```bash
Rscript -e 'library(data.table); str(fread("covid.csv", nrows = 1000))'                # fips: int
python3 -c 'import pandas as pd; print(pd.read_csv("covid.csv", nrows=1000).dtypes)'   # fips: float64 (the column has missing values)
```

3. **You must read everything to get anything.** A CSV is stored row by row, so a question about two columns still reads (and parses) all six. The lectures' `cut -d, -f3` has to scan every byte of every line to find the third comma.

Parquet stores the column types (text, integers, decimal numbers, dates and timestamps, true/false) in the file itself, so nobody has to guess them again. It also stores the columns separately, so a query can read only the columns it needs. A column with few distinct values (like the 55 states) is stored compactly as a small list of levels plus a short code per row (dictionary encoding).

## A short history

Parquet is not old, and it came out of a specific problem: companies with petabytes of logs on Hadoop clusters whose queries were slow because they read row after row of text.

+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      Year | What happened                                                                  |
+==========:+:===============================================================================+
|      2010 | Google publishes the **Dremel** paper: how to store even nested records *by    |
|           | column*, so a query touches only the columns it names. Google used it          |
|           | internally for web-scale analytics (it later became BigQuery).                 |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      2013 | **Twitter** and **Cloudera** (whose Impala engine needed a fast file format)   |
|           | build an open-source version of Dremel's storage ideas and call it Parquet.    |
|           | About the same time, Hive's **ORC** format appears with the same idea.         |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      2015 | Parquet becomes a top-level project of the Apache Software Foundation, the     |
|           | home of Hadoop and Spark.                                                      |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      2016 | **Apache Arrow**, started by Wes McKinney (the author of `pandas`), defines    |
|           | the same columnar layout *in memory*. Parquet on disk and Arrow in memory fit  |
|           | together, which is why Python and R can read Parquet so quickly.               |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      2017 | `pandas` gets `read_parquet` and `to_parquet`, and R gets the `arrow` package. |
|           | Parquet leaves the Hadoop world.                                               |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 2018-2019 | **Iceberg** (from Netflix) and **Delta Lake** (from Databricks) appear: table  |
|           | formats that add transactions and "undo" on top of folders of Parquet files.   |
|           | **DuckDB**, a database that queries a Parquet file directly, appears.          |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Dates are from my memory of the projects' histories; check the Apache Parquet site before quoting one.

## How popular is it?

There is no number like the "share of developers" we quoted for `git`, because nobody surveys file formats. What we can say is where it shows up, and that is nearly everywhere in data engineering:

* **Engines read and write it.** Spark writes Parquet by default, and Snowflake, BigQuery, AWS Athena and DuckDB all load, export or query it directly.
* **Table formats are built on it.** Delta Lake and Iceberg, the standard ways of organizing a company's folders of files into tables, default store their data *as Parquet files* plus a layer of bookkeeping.
* **Both our languages support it.** Python's `pandas`, `polars` and R's `arrow` read and write it, so a Parquet file made in Python opens in R unchanged. That makes it the format of choice for *handing data between tools*, unlike a `.pkl` or `.rds`.
* **Public data is published in it**, for example many datasets on the Hugging Face hub and large open datasets on cloud storage.

It has rivals: **ORC** (the same idea, mostly in the Hive world), **Avro** (row-based, popular for streams of events), and newer formats still being tested. But if you join a data team and ask "what format is the data in?", the most likely answer today is "Parquet".

## Converting `covid.csv`

First, say what each column *is*. In Python, `dtype` and `parse_dates` do it; then `to_parquet` writes the file (it needs the `pyarrow` package):

```{python}
import os
import pandas as pd
os.chdir(os.path.expanduser("~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03"))   # where covid.csv lives
df = pd.read_csv("covid.csv", dtype={"fips": str}, parse_dates=["date"])   # fips is a code (text), date is a date
print(df.dtypes)
df.to_parquet("covid_python.parquet", compression="zstd")
```

In R, the `arrow` package does the same. `schema(fips = string())` overrides the guess for just that column:

```{r}
library(arrow)
setwd("~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03")   # where covid.csv lives
df <- read_csv_arrow("covid.csv", col_types = schema(fips = string()))
write_parquet(df, "covid_R.parquet", compression = "zstd")
```

Now examine the parquet files:

```bash
ls -alh                             # 35M versus 3.3M
file covid_python.parquet           # Apache Parquet
file covid_R.parquet                # Apache Parquet
gzip -k covid.csv; ls -alh covid.csv.gz; rm covid.csv.gz     # recall from lec 2: 8.9M: the CSV zipped
head -c 4 covid_python.parquet; echo; tail -c 4 covid_python.parquet       # PAR1 at both ends: the "magic bytes"
```

The Parquet files are about **10 times smaller** than the CSV, and even smaller than the gzipped CSV, **and** they can be read directly. Are they exactly the same between R and Python?

+---------------------------+----------------------------+----------------------------+
|                           | `covid_R.parquet`          | `covid_python.parquet`     |
+:==========================+:===========================+:===========================+
| Writer                    | parquet-cpp-arrow 24.0.0   | parquet-cpp-arrow 25.0.1   |
+---------------------------+----------------------------+----------------------------+
| `date`                    | `date32` (a date)          | `timestamp[us]`            |
+---------------------------+----------------------------+----------------------------+
| `county`, `state`, `fips` | `string`                   | `large_string`             |
+---------------------------+----------------------------+----------------------------+
| `cases`                   | `int32`                    | `int64`                    |
+---------------------------+----------------------------+----------------------------+
| `deaths`                  | `int32`                    | `double`                   |
+---------------------------+----------------------------+----------------------------+
| Extra metadata            | none                       | a `pandas` metadata block  |
+---------------------------+----------------------------+----------------------------+

: The two Parquet files side by side. Same table, but each program chose its own column types a little bit differently, so the bytes differ. The values inside are identical. The two version of the parquet writers may differ in other ways as well. Nothing will change what comes next. 

Reading it back keeps the types, so `date` is still a date and `fips` is still the text `"06059"` without anybody guessing:

```python
pd.read_parquet("covid.parquet").dtypes
```

And you can ask for only the columns you want:

```python
pd.read_parquet("covid.parquet", columns=["state", "cases"])   # reads two of the six columns
```

Here are our timings on this file (the median of 7 runs on one machine; yours will differ but the ranking should not). For the CSV the package is `data.table::fread` in R and `pandas.read_csv` in Python; for Parquet it is the `arrow` package in R and `pandas.read_parquet` in Python (which uses `pyarrow` underneath):

+-------------------+----------------------------------+----------+----------+
| Task              | Package                          | CSV      | Parquet  |
+:==================+:=================================+=========:+=========:+
| File size         | (either package)                 | 35.9 MB  | 3.4 MB   |
+-------------------+----------------------------------+----------+----------+
| Read the whole    | R (`data.table` for CSV, `arrow` | 0.16 s   | 0.05 s   |
| table             | for Parquet)                     |          |          |
|                   +----------------------------------+----------+----------+
|                   | Python (`pandas`)                | 0.88 s   | 0.05 s   |
+-------------------+----------------------------------+----------+----------+
| Read only `state` | R (`data.table` for CSV, `arrow` | 0.09 s   | 0.03 s   |
| and `cases`       | for Parquet)                     |          |          |
|                   +----------------------------------+----------+----------+
|                   | Python (`pandas`)                | 0.37 s   | 0.02 s   |
+-------------------+----------------------------------+----------+----------+

: Reading `covid.csv` versus `covid.parquet`. The R Parquet times return an ordinary `data.frame`.

Notice that the CSV cannot make the two-column read much faster (`select=` and `usecols` still have to scan every line), while Parquet gets faster because it never touches the other columns.

Be fair to the CSV, though: `pandas` has a slow CSV reader, and R's `data.table::fread` is one of the fastest CSV readers there is. On this 35 MB file `fread` loads the whole table in 0.16 s, versus 0.05 s for the Parquet file. (If you then convert the Parquet result to a `data.table`, that conversion costs more than the read itself, and the total, 0.26 s, is slower than `fread`.) The columns-only read is where Parquet clearly wins (0.03 s versus 0.09 s). At 35 MB nobody should care about any of this. The real difference shows up when the file is much bigger, and that is the section after next.

One limitation by design:

* **Ordinal is where Parquet itself stops, on purpose.** Parquet's types say how values are *stored* (which bytes, which encoding), not what they *mean*. The grades A, B, C take the same bytes whether they are nominal or ordinal, and the rule "A is better than B" belongs to the program doing the analysis, so Parquet leaves it to the reader. (For the same reason, it does not separate interval from ratio.) `pandas` and `arrow` write the order into the file's metadata and read it back (we checked that an ordered `category` comes back ordered), but another tool reading the same file just sees text.

```bash
rm covid_R.parquet covid_python.parquet #cleanup
```

## When the data is really large

Everything above fits in memory on any laptop. So let us make a dataset that is 50 times bigger: `covid.csv` stacked 50 times, with a `copy` column saying which copy a row came from. That's' 44 million rows. (The numbers are copies of each other, so this is a toy dataset, but the size and the shape are real.) The script is in `lectures/scripts/lec03/` and writes the data twice: once as a single big CSV, and once as a single big Parquet file:

```bash
python3 ../../lectures/scripts/lec03/make_covid_big.py covid.csv 50 --csv   # about 80 seconds
ls -alh # 1.8G raw CSV vs 163M parquet
```

The question for both versions: *what is the total of `cases` in Texas, separately for every copy?*

We will not examine the R/Python code for this as we will leave it for another lecture. Here are the results, split into the time to **load** the data and the time to **ask** the question (median of 3 runs on a 12-core machine with 41 GB of memory, with the file already in the operating system's cache; yours will differ but the ranking should not). every tool that can use several cores (`fread`, the `pyarrow` CSV reader in `pandas`, `arrow` and `pyarrow`) was limited to 6 threads, which is the default of `data.table`, so the comparison is fair (`awk` always uses one). A tool that streams (`awk`) or reads lazily (`arrow`) has no load step:

+------------------+-------------------------------+--------------+---------+---------+-------------+
| Format           | Tool                          | Load         | Ask     | Total   | Peak memory |
+:=================+:==============================+=============:+========:+========:+============:+
| CSV (1.8 GB)     | R: `data.table::fread`        | 13.8 s       | 2.0 s   | 15.8 s  | 3.5 GB      |
|                  +-------------------------------+--------------+---------+---------+-------------+
|                  | Python: `pandas` with         | 8.2 s        | 3.8 s   | 12.0 s  | 6.1 GB      |
|                  | `engine="pyarrow"`            |              |         |         |             |
|                  +-------------------------------+--------------+---------+---------+-------------+
|                  | `awk` (`gawk`)                | none         | 64 s    | 64 s    | 5 MB        |
|                  +-------------------------------+--------------+---------+---------+-------------+
|                  | `awk` (`mawk`)[^mawk]         | none         | 20 s    | 20 s    | 3 MB        |
+------------------+-------------------------------+--------------+---------+---------+-------------+
| Parquet (163 MB) | R: `arrow`                    | none         | 1.7 s   | 1.7 s   | 0.5 GB      |
|                  +-------------------------------+--------------+---------+---------+-------------+
|                  | Python: `pyarrow`             | none         | 1.1 s   | 1.1 s   | 0.5 GB      |
+------------------+-------------------------------+--------------+---------+---------+-------------+

: The same question on the CSV and on the Parquet file. Peak memory is the most that Linux reports the whole run used. The machine was also busy with other work during these runs, so the times are on the slow side; the ranking is what matters.

[^mawk]: `mawk` is a different implementation of `awk` that is faster than the default `gawk` on massive datasets (about three times faster here), and it runs the same programs: the syntax of everything in this course is identical. It lacks some GNU-only extras (for example the functions `asort` and `gensub`). We are not covering it officially but if you want to use it, install it with `sudo apt install mawk` (on a Mac: `brew install mawk`) and run `mawk` in place of `awk`.

With its default CSV reader, `pandas` is much slower: 80 s to load (about 85 s in total) and 5.4 GB. 

WARNING*** `pandas engine="pyarrow"`: it guesses the type of every column itself, so it turns `fips` into a number and drops the leading zero (e.g., `06001` becomes `6001`). That could be bad - double check always your data types when loading CSVs!!

Read the Load and memory columns carefully. `fread` and `pandas` need several gigabytes *because they load all the data first*, and that is the number that decides whether your laptop can do the job at all. On a laptop with 8 GB of memory and a file double or triple this size, they simply fail with "out of memory". `awk` and the Parquet versions never hold the whole data: `awk` keeps only a running total for each `copy` (megabytes), and `arrow` streams through the file a piece at a time and keeps only the running totals (about 0.5 GB). The same code would work on a 500 GB file. (The 163 MB is flattering: the 50 copies are identical, which compresses much better than real data does. The memory and the speed advantage are the real result.)

How can parquet be this much faster? The annotations again:

* It read **3 of the 7 columns** (`state`, `cases`, `copy`) and never touched the others.
* It used the **row-group statistics** to skip blocks that cannot contain Texas.
* It processed **one row group at a time**, so memory never held the whole dataset.
* It can skip row groups using the `copy` column's min and max. Each copy is its own row group, so asking only about the first five copies reads only five of the 50 row groups. That took 0.5 s in R and 0.13 s in Python on our machine (versus 1.7 s and 1.1 s for all 50):

```r
open_dataset("covid_big.parquet") |> filter(state == "Texas", copy < 5) |> group_by(copy) |> summarise(cases = sum(cases)) |> collect()
```

(Parquet can also be split over many files, one folder per value of a column, so whole files can be skipped. That is called *partitioning*, and we will return to it in a later lecture.)

The same file can be asked with SQL by DuckDB, a database that runs on Parquet files and is available in both R and Python. In R, the `duckdb` package (also with 6 threads) gave the same answer in 0.9 s:

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT copy, sum(cases) AS cases
                      FROM read_parquet('covid_big.parquet')
                      WHERE state = 'Texas' GROUP BY copy")
```

### Can't `awk` do this in constant memory?

Yes, and that is a fair objection, because a streaming tool never loads the data. Count the rows in each state, first with `awk` on the CSV and then with `arrow` on the Parquet file:

```bash
awk -F, 'NR>1 {n[$3]++} END {for (s in n) print s "," n[s]}' covid_big.csv | sort -t, -k2,2nr | head -n 3
```

```r
open_dataset("covid_big.parquet") |> count(state) |> arrange(desc(n)) |> collect()
```

Both give the same answer (Texas 3,350,100, Georgia 2,260,450, Virginia 1,844,300). We also timed a second question with each tool, the total of Texas `cases` for each `copy`:

+--------------------------------------+---------------------+-----------------------+
|                                      | `awk` on the CSV    | `arrow` on Parquet    |
+:=====================================+====================:+======================:+
| Rows per state: time                 | 68 s                | 1.5 s                 |
+--------------------------------------+---------------------+-----------------------+
| Texas cases per copy: time           | 64 s                | 1.7 s                 |
+--------------------------------------+---------------------+-----------------------+
| Peak memory (rows per state)         | 4.6 MB              | 420 MB                |
+--------------------------------------+---------------------+-----------------------+

: One run, one machine. `awk` uses one core, `arrow` uses six.

On memory, `awk` wins by a factor of nearly a hundred: 4.6 MB, because it keeps only a counter for each of the 55 states. The price is **time**. `awk` has to read and split every one of the 1.8 GB for *every* question, so each question costs about a minute, and ten questions cost more than ten minutes (`mawk` is about three times faster than `gawk` here, so about 20 s per question). `arrow` answered in about two seconds, because the first question needed only the `state` column (one of seven) and it spread the work over several cores. Converting the CSV to Parquet costs one pass, once, and then every later question is cheap.

Streaming also has limits that Parquet does not. `awk` stays at constant memory only when the number of groups is small: a table of 44 million different keys would not fit in a hash map. A median needs all the values, a sort needs temporary files, and a join needs one of the two tables in memory. And as the `cut` example earlier showed, it breaks on a CSV with quoted fields (note that we had to turn quoting off to write `covid_big.csv`, or `awk` would see `"Texas"` with the quotes).

So the honest rule is: for a single question about a file you will read once, `awk` on the CSV is fine and Parquet does not help. Parquet pays off when you will ask **many** questions about the **same** large table, and when each question touches only some of its columns.

Clean up the big files when you are done, since they take about 2 GB: `rm covid_big.parquet covid_big.csv`.

## What it cannot do

* **It is binary.** `head`, `grep`, `cut` and `awk` show gibberish. You need a program that understands Parquet, which is why the shell tools from lectures 1 and 2 are for the *before* step and Parquet is for the *after*.
* **It is write-once.** You cannot change one value in place or append a row to the file; you rewrite it. (Delta Lake and Iceberg exist to hide this.)
* **It is still just a file.** It has no indexes, no users, and nothing stops two programs from writing at once. For that you need a database, which is next.

## Which format when?

Putting the four formats side by side, for tabular data like `covid.csv`. A ✓ means "best of the four, or tied for best", ✗ means "poor or missing", and *partly* is in between. The sizes are for the whole `covid.csv` (the JSON size is from the lecture 2 benchmark).

+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
|                  | CSV            | CSV + `xz`     | JSON             | Parquet       |
+:=================+:==============:+:==============:+:================:+:=============:+
| Human-readable   | ✓              | ✗              | ✓                | ✗             |
| in a text editor |                |                |                  |               |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Opens            | ✓              | partly         | ✓                | ✗             |
| everywhere, no   |                |                |                  |               |
| special library  |                |                |                  |               |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Smallest file    | ✗ 35.9 MB      | ✓ 1.8 MB       | ✗ about 94 MB    | ✗ 3.4 MB      |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Column types     | ✗              | ✗              | partly           | ✓             |
| stored in the    |                |                |                  |               |
| file             |                |                |                  |               |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Load the whole   | ✓              | ✗              | ✗                | ✓             |
| table fast       |                |                |                  |               |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Read only some   | ✗              | ✗              | ✗                | ✓             |
| columns fast     |                |                |                  |               |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Skip data using  | ✗              | ✗              | ✗                | ✓             |
| built-in         |                |                |                  |               |
| summaries        |                |                |                  |               |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Query data       | partly         | partly         | ✗                | ✓             |
| bigger than      |                |                |                  |               |
| memory           |                |                |                  |               |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Append a row     | ✓              | ✗              | partly           | ✗             |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Nested records   | ✗              | ✗              | ✓                | ✓             |
| (lists inside    |                |                |                  |               |
| records)         |                |                |                  |               |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Works with       | ✓              | ✓ with `xzcat` | partly           | ✗             |
| `grep`, `cut`,   |                |                |                  |               |
| `awk` in a pipe  |                |                |                  |               |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+
| Best for         | handing small  | archiving and  | web APIs, nested | analyzing big |
|                  | data to anyone | sending        | data             | tabular data  |
+------------------+----------------+----------------+------------------+---------------+

: Notes: JSON gets *partly* for appending because a JSON Lines file (one record per line) can be appended to, but an ordinary JSON array cannot. CSV and CSV + `xz` get *partly* for bigger-than-memory queries because `awk` and friends stream through the file, but they have to read all of it, every time.

No format wins every row. CSV wins on universality, `xz` on size, JSON on nesting, and Parquet wins on everything about *reading a lot of tabular data quickly*, which is why it is the one that data engineers choose for analysis.

# Databases: when a CSV is not enough

A CSV is a fine way to *ship* data, and the tools from the last two lectures are fine for a quick look. But as soon as you ask many questions of the same data, or change it, or share it, the file starts to hurt. In this unit we feel the pain first, and then fix it with a **database**: a program that stores data in a structured way and answers questions about it quickly. We will use **PostgreSQL** ("Postgres"), which you installed in the setup guide.

We keep working in the same scratch folder as the Parquet unit above (`scratch/lec03`, with `covid.csv` in it).

## Where a CSV hurts

**1. Every question is a full scan.** A CSV has no way to jump to the rows you want, so each question reads the whole file from the top:

```bash
time awk -F, '$3=="Texas" && $2=="Harris"' covid.csv | wc -l   # about 1.3 s
time awk -F, '$3=="Texas" && $2=="Harris"' covid.csv | wc -l   # again: same
```

The second run is no faster than the first. On this 35 MB file a second is fine. On a 35 GB file it is twenty minutes, **for every question you ask**.

**2. The file doesn't know what the data means.** To `grep` and `awk`, a CSV is just text. Recall that `grep Texas` counts 67,497 rows while the right answer is 67,002: it also counted the 495 rows of Texas *County*, in Missouri and Oklahoma. And nothing stops a `cases` column from containing `N/A` or an empty string.

**3. Changing one value means rewriting the file.** To fix a single number in the middle of a CSV, `sed -i` reads and writes the entire file.

**4. Several people or programs at once.** Two jobs appending to the same CSV at the same time can interleave their lines and corrupt it. There is no protection if the machine crashes halfway through a write.

**5. Combining files.** Adding each state's population to every row needs a second CSV and a `join`, with both files sorted first.

One more thing is *not* a problem. **Adding a line to a CSV is very fast**, faster than inserting into a database. Databases pay for their structure when you load data, and win when you ask questions.

## Connecting to PostgreSQL

Check that the server is running and that you can log in:

```bash
psql -c "SELECT version();"      # a line starting with: PostgreSQL 18
```

Notice that no password was needed. Your setup created a database user with the same name as your Linux user, and the server trusts connections made from your own machine by that user. (This is how Postgres is set up on a standard Ubuntu or Homebrew install. It is **not** how you will reach a remote database, which will ask for a password or a key.)

Make a database for this lecture and open the SQL prompt in it:

```bash
createdb lec03                   # a new, empty database
psql lec03                       # the interactive prompt; \q quits
```

A few commands that start with a backslash belong to `psql` itself and are not SQL:

+--------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| Command      | What it does                                  |
+==============+===============================================+
| `\timing on` | print how long each statement took            |
+--------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `\d covid`   | describe a table: its columns and their types |
+--------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `\dt`        | list the tables                               |
+--------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `\q`         | quit                                          |
+--------------+-----------------------------------------------+

## Loading the CSV

A database table has **typed columns**. We state them up front and then load the file with `\copy`, which reads a file on *your* machine:

```sql
\timing on
CREATE TABLE covid (
  date   date,
  county text,
  state  text,
  fips   text,
  cases  integer,
  deaths integer
);
\copy covid FROM 'covid.csv' CSV HEADER
SELECT count(*) FROM covid;      -- 884737, the same as wc -l minus the header
```

`CSV HEADER` tells Postgres that the first line holds column names and not data. The load takes about a second. (Use `\copy` and not plain `COPY`. `COPY` makes the *server* read the file, and the server is a different user who is not allowed into your home folder.)

## Asking questions

SQL describes *what* you want, not how to loop over lines. The questions from earlier lectures become:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM covid WHERE state = 'Texas';           -- 67002
SELECT max(cases) FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris';              -- 237727
SELECT state, count(*) FROM covid
  GROUP BY state ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 5;            -- top 5 states
```

The first answer is exactly 67,002 with no regular expression and no counting of the wrong column. Because each column has a name and a type, `state = 'Texas'` cannot match a county. These queries take about 60 to 90 ms: faster than `awk`, but still reading the entire table. The real speed-up comes next.

## Indexes

An **index** is a sorted lookup structure that the database keeps beside the table, like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find "Harris", it looks up the entry and jumps to the right pages.

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT max(cases) FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris';
```

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows how Postgres ran the query. Without an index you will see `Seq Scan` (a *sequential scan*: reading every row) and an execution time of about 70 ms. Now create the index and run the same `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` again:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON covid (state, county);     -- takes about a second, once
```

The plan changes to an `Index Scan` (or `Bitmap Index Scan`) and the time drops to **under 1 ms**. The table has 884,737 rows, and the database looked at about 300 of them.

The time to answer is now almost independent of the table's size. That is the reason databases exist. The cost is paid once, when you build the index (about 1.2 seconds here), plus a little extra on every insert to keep the index up to date and some extra disk space.

## The database checks your data

Try to add a row with a nonsense value:

```sql
INSERT INTO covid VALUES ('2021-01-01', 'Harris', 'Texas', '48201', 'N/A', 0);
-- ERROR:  invalid input syntax for type integer: "N/A"
```

A CSV would have accepted that line without complaint, and the problem would have appeared much later, in the middle of an analysis. A database refuses bad data at the door. Types are the simplest of its guarantees. Later you can add rules such as `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE` and `CHECK`.

## Changing data

Fixing one value touches only the rows you name:

```sql
UPDATE covid SET deaths = deaths + 1
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris' AND date = '2020-12-31';
```

Compare that with `sed -i` on a 35 GB file. You can also wrap several changes in a **transaction** (`BEGIN; ... COMMIT;`), and either all of them happen or none of them do. If the machine crashes halfway through, the database recovers to a consistent state.

## Using the database from the shell

You do not need the interactive prompt. `psql -c` runs one statement, and the output can feed straight back into the pipes you already know:

```bash
psql lec03 -c "SELECT count(*) FROM covid"
psql lec03 -At -c "SELECT county FROM covid WHERE state='Utah'" | sort -u
psql lec03 -c "\copy (SELECT * FROM covid WHERE state='Utah') \
  TO 'utah.csv' CSV HEADER"
```

`-A` turns off the table formatting and `-t` removes headers and footers, which leaves plain lines for `sort`, `wc` and friends. The last line goes the other way and writes the result of a query out as a CSV.

## What did you install?

Postgres is a lot of software. Add it up, with `du` ("disk usage") for the program files and the database itself for your data:

```bash
du -ch /usr/lib/postgresql /usr/share/postgresql | tail -n 1   # the program
psql -At -c "SELECT pg_size_pretty(sum(pg_database_size(datname)))
             FROM pg_database"                          # all your data
```

`du -c` adds a grand total at the end and `tail -n 1` keeps only that line. On Ubuntu the program is about 50 MB. (On a Mac with Homebrew, use `du -shL "$(brew --prefix postgresql@18)"`.) The `covid` table alone took about 63 MB with its index, almost twice the 35 MB CSV.

That is a lot of space for a program whose job is to store rows. But look at what it bought you in this unit:

- **Speed:** the same question went from 1.3 s with `awk` to under 1 ms with an index, and that stays true as the table grows.
- **Correctness:** typed columns refused `'N/A'` as a number, and `state = 'Texas'` could not match a county.
- **Safe changes:** single-row updates and transactions that happen completely or not at all, even if the machine crashes.
- **Many users at once:** many programs reading and writing the same tables at once without corrupting them.
- **A query language** instead of one-off shell pipelines: SQL, with joins, grouping and sorting, and a planner that picks how to run each query.

PostgreSQL grew out of research at Berkeley in the 1980s and has had decades of engineering since. Nobody would write all of that again for one analysis. That is why it is worth the space: you get it for free, and it is already installed.

## Clean up

```bash
dropdb lec03                     # delete the whole database
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it
1. Find the five counties with the highest `deaths` on 2020-12-31, as a single SQL statement (`ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`). Your first attempt will probably list counties with *no* number at all. Some rows in the CSV have an empty `deaths`, which the database stores as `NULL`, and `ORDER BY ... DESC` puts `NULL` first. Fix it with `NULLS LAST`.
2. Time the query "maximum `cases` in Harris, Texas" with and without the index (`DROP INDEX` to remove it). Then do the same with `awk` on the CSV. How many times faster is the indexed query?
3. Load the CSV again into a second table, but declare `cases` as `text`. What changes, and which of the queries above breaks or gives wrong answers? (Try `max(cases)`: as text, `'9999'` sorts after `'237727'`.)
:::
